articles.title_original: A proposal for a hybrid free-space optical quantum communication network with hexagonal boron nitride-based single photon sources
articles.title_en: Proposal for hBN-Based Satellite Quantum Communication Network
articles.excerpt_original: Hexagonal boron nitride (hBN) is known as a promising solid-state platform to host room temperature quantum emitters that produce high purity single photons. The bright and spectrally adaptable hBN emitters are space-compatible, making hBN well-suited for satellite-based free-space optical (FSO) quantum key distribution (QKD) at wavelengths where the atmospheric background is naturally suppressed. This paper presents a pathway to develop hBN emitters operating near the Ca-II Fraunhofer line (at 854 nm), enabling daylight FSO operation. Moreover, due to its compatibility with the first telecommunication window at 850 nm, it is possible to interface with optical fibers to bridge the `last mile' in a scenario where multiple end-users connect through a single optical ground station to a QKD satellite. We therefore introduce a concept that combines continuous operation of a quantum network, hybrid links to minimize deployment costs, and high data rates due to the use of realistic single photon sources. The realization would be an important milestone for the development of the quantum internet.
articles.summary_en: Researchers propose a hybrid free-space optical quantum key distribution network using hexagonal boron nitride single-photon sources operating near 854 nm. The concept combines satellite links, optical-fiber connectivity and daylight operation to support future quantum-internet infrastructure.

articles.title_original: Persistence and emergence of quantum defects through pressure-induced phase changes
articles.title_en: Pressure-Resilient Quantum Sensors Demonstrated in Boron Nitride
articles.excerpt_original: Extreme pressures can transform materials and their properties, but probing these in-situ is made challenging by the small sample volumes and access requirements demanded by diamond anvil cells. Quantum defects offer a route to local measurements under such conditions, yet their sensing performance can be dictated by pressure-induced changes in their own host material. On the other hand, pressure may also be harnessed as a tool to engineer and stabilize new quantum defects with emergent functionalities. Here, we demonstrate both aspects within a unified platform based on optically active spin-pair defects in hexagonal boron nitride (hBN). As robust quantum sensors under pressure, these spin-1/2 systems retain pressure-independent spin resonances up to 20 GPa while maintaining or even enhancing their optical emission, in stark contrast to the spin-1 boron-vacancy centre in the same material. Simultaneously, we show that compression acts as a means of quantum defect engineering: the starting hBN undergoes an irreversible transformation into wurtzite boron nitride (wBN), during which the defect landscape is reconfigured. Spin-pair sensors are seen to persist across this structural transition, however, depending on the starting material we also observe new, highly fluorescent defects in the wBN phase. These results establish spin-pair defects in boron nitride as pressure-resilient quantum sensors while highlighting high pressure itself as a versatile pathway for creating and tuning quantum emitters.
articles.summary_en: Researchers show that spin-pair defects in hexagonal boron nitride retain stable spin resonances up to 20 GPa while maintaining or enhancing optical emission. Pressure also drives transformation to wurtzite boron nitride and generates new fluorescent defects, indicating a route to engineer quantum emitters.

articles.title_original: Twist as a Mechanical Switch for Reconfigurable Stacking in h-BN
articles.title_en: Twist Mechanically Switches h-BN Stacking States
articles.excerpt_original: Twistronics of layered materials has emerged as a highly active field due to its profound implications for quantum electronics and materials engineering. However, the controllable manipulation of interlayer stacking remains a significant experimental challenge. Here, the homogeneous contact between hexagonal boron nitride layers is shown to be reproducibly switched between two distinct stable stacking configurations via an externally applied torque. Combining experiments and computational modelling, we identify the stacking order of these stable states as the commensurate AA and AB modes. These two states are associated with different rotational torque maxima, exhibiting an asymmetry ratio of 0.7, and distinct dynamics as a function of the twist angle. Moreover, the peak torque values scale linearly with contact area, highlighting the dominant role of edge elasticity in the twisting process. Given that the AA and AB stacking modes correspond to different out-of-plane electric polarization states, our findings offer a pathway for reconfigurable nano- and micro-electromechanical devices.
articles.summary_en: Researchers demonstrated reversible switching between AA and AB stacking in layered hexagonal boron nitride using externally applied torque. The distinct polarization states could enable reconfigurable nano- and micro-electromechanical devices.

articles.title_original: Tailoring mechanical and dielectric behaviours of basalt fiber/epoxy composites via dual ceramic fillers incorporation and Grey–Taguchi optimization
articles.title_en: Basalt–Epoxy Composites Enhanced with Alumina and Hexagonal Boron Nitride
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract For several decades, epoxy thermoset resins have been widely used as dielectric materials in high-voltage electrical insulation systems. However, today''s needs require improved thermal, dielectric and mechanical performances from these materials. Hence the use of basalt fibre reinforcement, in addition to ceramic fillers, is explored to improve the properties of the epoxy composites. This research paper presents a study on the mechanical and electrical performances of hexagonal boron nitride and alumina ceramic fillers/basalt fiber/epoxy composites via experimental method and then utilises Grey Relational Analysis (GRA) to optimise multiple responses based on the input variables of filler weight percentage. The basalt fiber/ceramic fillers reinforced hybrid epoxy composites (BF/CF/HEC) are manufactured using hand lay-up method with compression mould. L9 orthogonal array design is employed with filler loadings of 2.5%, 5% and 7.5% by weight. The impacts of hybrid filler content on ultimate tensile strength (UTS), Izod impact strength and dielectric constant (DC) are investigated. The experimental findings show a significant relationship between mechanical properties and electrical performance with respect to the dispersion of fillers and the interfacial bonding between the fillers and the epoxy matrix. BF/CF/HEC5 exhibits 50.4% higher UTS and the highest Young’s modulus of 8119 MPa, indicating superior tensile strength and stiffness. The composite, having a balanced composition of alumina and hBN, exhibits higher UTS due to better stress transfer mechanisms and crack deflection mechanisms. articles.summary_en: Researchers optimized basalt fiber/epoxy composites containing alumina and hexagonal boron nitride ceramic fillers for mechanical and dielectric performance. An optimized formulation achieved 50.4% higher ultimate tensile strength and a Young’s modulus of 8,119 MPa.

articles.title_original: 2D Covalent Organic Frameworks as Robust n‐Type Organic Mixed Ionic‐Electronic Conductors for Electrochemical Transistors
articles.title_en: 2D Covalent Organic Frameworks Enable Stable n-Type Electrochemical Transistors
articles.excerpt_original: ABSTRACT Organic mixed ionic‐electronic conductors (OMIECs) with exclusive electrochemical modulation and coupling between ions and electrons have exhibited intriguing efficiencies in bioelectronics, logic circuits, and wearable devices. However, OMIECs are typically linear polymers whose excessive structural swelling and morphological disorder during electrochemical doping led to low performance and instability. Here, we report n‐type 2D covalent organic frameworks (2D COFs) as novel OMIECs (BTID‐BFDO COF and BTDD‐BFDO COF). The rigid π‐conjugated scaffold functions as both a charge transport pathway and an ion‐electron coupling plane, whilst the nanochannels serve as directional conduits for rapid ion transport. 2D OMIECs‐based OECTs exhibit favorable threshold voltages (< 0.5 V), I on /I off ratios (10 3 ) and high stability (modulation current retention rate of 91.3% during continuous operation) compared with the linear counterpart (< 10%). More importantly, we elucidate the mechanism underlying in situ ion transport and doping within the rigid porous architectures of 2D OMIECs, establishing a novel design paradigm for robust n‐type organic semiconductors.
articles.summary_en: Researchers developed rigid 2D covalent organic frameworks as n-type organic mixed ionic-electronic conductors, using π-conjugated scaffolds for charge transport and nanochannels for ion transport. Devices showed threshold voltages below 0.5 V, on/off ratios of 10³, and 91.3% current retention during continuous operation, outperforming linear-polymer counterparts.

articles.title_original: Facile Fabrication of 2D/0D ZnSe/ZnO Heterostructures for Efficient Photocatalytic Degradation of Organic Dye
articles.title_en: ZnSe/ZnO Heterostructures Improve Photocatalytic Dye Degradation
articles.excerpt_original: In order to improve the light absorption capacity of ZnO and inhibit the recombination of photogenerated charge carriers, we prepared ZnSe/ZnO heterostructures using a simple electrostatic self‐assembly method. The experimental results showed that 0D ZnO nanoparticles (NPs) were successfully loaded onto the surface of 2D ZnSe nanosheets (NSs), forming heterostructures. This composite structure increased the number of reactive adsorption–desorption sites, which was beneficial for accelerating the photocatalytic reaction rate. The 3D open skeleton composite structure of ZnSe NSs/ZnO NPs helped to improve the utilization efficiency of incident light in photocatalytic processes. In addition, the energy bands of ZnSe NSs and ZnO NPs are arranged in a staggered manner, forming a typical Type‐II semiconductor heterostructure, effectively inhibiting the recombination of photogenerated charge carriers. We also investigated the relationship between component ratio and photocatalytic activity. Under UV and visible light irradiation, the ZnSe NSs/ZnO NPs nanocomposites (ZZ5) showed significantly higher photocatalytic degradation efficiency for the organic dye RhB than pure ZnO NPs, achieving over 90%. This enhancement is attributed to the optimal component ratio, which is conducive to the separation of photogenerated charge carriers and improves the utilization efficiency of incident light.
articles.summary_en: Researchers fabricated 2D/0D ZnSe/ZnO heterostructures through electrostatic self-assembly, improving light utilization and charge-carrier separation. The optimized composite degraded more than 90% of Rhodamine B under UV and visible light, indicating potential for photocatalytic treatment applications.

articles.title_original: INFLUENCE OF GRAPHENE OXIDE ON THE PROPERTIES OF POLYPROPYLENE NANOCOMPOSITES
articles.title_en: Graphene Oxide Improves Strength and Hydrophobicity of Polypropylene Nanocomposites
articles.excerpt_original: In this work, the influence of small concentrations of graphene oxide on the physicomechanical properties of nanocomposites based on polypropylene and polyester oil was studied. A nano dispersed filler was added to the polypropylene matrix in amounts of 0.01 %, 0.05 % and 0.1 %. A rotary mixer with adjustable speed was used to homogenize the mixtures. To determine the characteristics of the new nanocomposite, test specimens were manufactured in accordance with EN 527 - 2 using the injection molding method. From the studies conducted, it was found that the introduction of graphene oxide nanoparticles into the polyolefin matrix in amounts of 0.01 %, 0.05 % and 0.1 % did not significantly affect the temperature-phase transitions. The addition of 0.1 % filler increased the hydrophobicityof polypropylene by 8 %, the tensile strength at break increased by 14 %. There is a tendency towards an increase in the fluidity of the composite materials, but in general it can be concluded that the filler in these quantities does not significantly change the rheology of the polymer material. The filler has an impact on the thermal conductivity properties of the compound, since the graphene particles serve as nuclei for crystal formation.
articles.summary_en: A study found that adding 0.1% graphene oxide to polypropylene increased tensile strength at break by 14% and hydrophobicity by 8%, while having little effect on phase transitions or rheology. The particles also acted as crystallization nuclei and influenced thermal conductivity, supporting graphene oxide’s use as a low-loading polymer composite additive.

articles.title_original: Understanding Graphene-Perovskite Interactions: From Flake Chemistry to Crystallisation and Solar Cell Performance
articles.title_en: Pristine Graphene Improves Perovskite Solar-Cell Efficiency and Stability
articles.excerpt_original: Graphene-derivatives are widely employed materials to improve bulk and interface properties of metal-halide perovskite devices. Yet the implications of their flake chemistry and interactions with the perovskite precursors remain unclear. Here, we show that pristine graphene flakes (GF) and more conventional graphene oxide flakes (GOF) are not interchangeable. Density functional theory calculations reveal that GOF interacts more strongly with the perovskite lattice but induces larger structural distortions, stronger interfacial polarisation, and localised gap states. In contrast, GF forms comparatively non-disruptive contacts, a response retained across a wide compositional range. Machine-learning atomistic simulations further show that GF contacts both Pb- and I-containing regions of solvated perovskite nanocrystals, with a strong solvent dependency. Solution spectroscopic characterization indicates that GF additives serve as scaffold for preorganised Pb/I-containing precursors, favouring film crystallisation. In this sense, GF enhances solar cell performance across perovskite compositions, but particularly those facing a more challenging crystallisation. In mixed Sn-Pb perovskite solar cells, GF raises the champion power-conversion efficiency from 21.5\% to 23.7\% with improved storage stability. These results establish pristine GF as a chemically defined additive and connect its atomic-scale interactions with precursor organisation, crystallisation, device performance, and stability.
articles.summary_en: A study finds pristine graphene flakes interact less disruptively with metal-halide perovskites than graphene oxide and can scaffold precursor organisation to promote crystallisation. In mixed tin–lead perovskite cells, graphene increased champion power-conversion efficiency from 21.5% to 23.7% and improved storage stability.

articles.title_original: A Wannier-first approach for extended chiral systems
articles.title_en: Wannier-first method enables efficient modeling of chiral graphene systems
articles.excerpt_original: We present a real-space formulation of DFT for extended systems in which localized Wannier-like functions are constructed directly from localized Gaussian basis functions without explicitly computing canonical Bloch-like states during the self-consistent cycle. Building on the formalism of Pederson and Lin [Phys. Rev. B \textbf{35}, 2273 (1987)], a variational set of Wannier-like functions is generated self-consistently within a finite Wannier domain and used to construct the charge density, electrostatic potential, and per cell total energy of the extended system. The occupied space can be determined entirely from the Wannier-like functions. Electronic band structures can be recovered in a post-processing step by solving the full Hamiltonian in a Bloch-like basis constructed from Gaussian orbitals. A key feature of the method is that it can incorporate combined translation--rotation, or screw, symmetries, enabling efficient simulations of chiral and helical systems with finite twist angles at essentially the same computational cost as systems described by pure translational symmetry. The approach is validated through calculations on linear and twisted $\mathrm{{-}C{\equiv}C{-}}$ and $\mathrm{{-}Li{-}F{-}}$ chains, as well as graphene, where total energies and band structures show excellent agreement with reference periodic calculations. To illustrate the ability of the method to treat three-dimensional systems, it is further applied to AA graphite, in which carbon atoms in adjacent graphene layers are aligned directly above one another, as well as helically stacked AA graphite structures. The Wannier-first framework provides a practical route for treating extended systems with nontrivial translational, rotational, and screw symmetries, and provides a natural foundation
articles.summary_en: Researchers present a real-space DFT framework that constructs localized Wannier-like functions without canonical Bloch states during self-consistent calculations. The method incorporates screw symmetries and accurately models graphene, AA graphite, and helically stacked graphite.

articles.title_original: Direct Observation of the Zigzag Edge States of a Supramolecular Diatomic Kagome Lattice
articles.title_en: Direct Observation of Graphene-Like Zigzag Edge States in a Diatomic Kagome Lattice
articles.excerpt_original: Lattice geometry plays a fundamental role in the behavior of Bloch electrons in a crystal. The diatomic Kagome lattice, an extension of the honeycomb and Kagome lattices, is predicted to give rise to emergent and topological phenomena, but its experimental investigation has been limited thus far. Here, we fabricate a diatomic Kagome lattice through self-assembly of a triptycene derivative with phenazine moieties (Trip-Phz)---a $\mathrm{C_3}$-symmetric, non-planar $π$-conjugated molecule. Our scanning tunneling microscopy (STM) observations show that Trip-Phz forms a highly ordered diatomic Kagome lattice terminated by zigzag-type edges on the Pb(111) surface. Combined STM measurements and tight-binding calculations provide direct evidence for the existence of the edge states that correspond to those of graphene. These states are topological edge states dictated by the quantization of the Zak phase and the bulk-edge correspondence.This work reveals an ideal platform for exploring quantum materials with unique lattice geometries using supramolecular technology.
articles.summary_en: Researchers fabricated a supramolecular diatomic Kagome lattice from a triptycene–phenazine molecule on Pb(111). Scanning tunneling microscopy and tight-binding calculations directly identified topological zigzag edge states analogous to those in graphene, providing a platform for studying quantum materials.

articles.title_en: Review Examines MXene Quantum Dots for High-Performance Supercapacitors
articles.excerpt_original: MXene quantum dots (MXQDs), produced by downsizing two-dimensional MXenes into zero-dimensional nanostructures, have emerged as promising materials for next-generation supercapacitors owing to their quantum confinement, metallic conductivity, abundant surface terminations, and excellent dispersibility. This review summarizes recent advances in MXQDs with emphasis on the synthesis structure-property-performance relationship governing their electrochemical behavior. Various synthesis strategies, including hydrothermal, microwave-assisted, laser-induced, and acousto-microfluidic methods, are discussed in relation to their effects on size, crystallinity, morphology, and surface chemistry. Advanced characterization techniques, including XRD, Raman, FTIR, TEM/HRTEM, and AFM, are highlighted for elucidating crystal structure, defect states, and surface functional groups. The effects of quantum confinement, heteroatom doping, defect engineering, and surface terminations on charge-transfer kinetics, ion diffusion, and pseudocapacitive behavior are critically examined. Furthermore, recent developments in MXQD-based electrode architectures, including carbon-, hydroxide-, and conducting polymer-based composites, as well as flexible and transparent supercapacitors, are evaluated with respect to their electrochemical performance. Finally, the remaining challenges, including precise control of surface terminations, aggregation, long-term stability, and scalable synthesis, are discussed together with future perspectives for the rational design and practical implementation of high-performance MXQD-based supercapacitors.
articles.summary_en: This academic review surveys MXene quantum dots (MXQDs), including their synthesis, electrochemical mechanisms, electrode architectures, and use in flexible and transparent supercapacitors. It identifies surface-termination control, aggregation, stability, and scalable production as key remaining challenges.

articles.title_original: Quantized heat flow in moiré chern bands of bilayer graphene
articles.title_en: Bilayer graphene reveals quantized heat flow in moiré Chern bands
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract When electrons are subjected simultaneously to a magnetic field and a periodic potential, they form the fractal Hofstadter spectrum, whose topological gaps host quantum Hall and Chern insulating states with distinct Chern numbers. While electrical transport has established the topology of these states, whether their heat transport is likewise universal has remained unexplored. Here, we measure the thermal conductance of quantum Hall, Chern insulator, and interaction-driven symmetry-broken Chern insulator states in a bilayer graphene-hexagonal boron nitride moiré superlattice with a moiré wavelength of ~14 nm using Johnson-noise thermometry. We find that the thermal conductance (G Q ) is quantized in units of the thermal conductance quantum (G Q = tκ 0 T) and is determined solely by the Chern number (t), independent of the microscopic origin of the topological state. By directly revealing universal topological heat transport in Hofstadter bands, our work establishes thermal conductance as a stringent probe of moiré topological matter and provides a route to investigating more exotic phases, including fractional Chern insulators.
articles.summary_en: Researchers measured thermal conductance in bilayer graphene–hexagonal boron nitride moiré superlattices and found it quantized according to the system’s Chern number. The result establishes thermal transport as a probe of topological states and may support investigations of fractional Chern insulators.

articles.title_original: Interferometry reveals spin-singlet fractional quantum Hall edges in graphene
articles.title_en: Interferometry reveals spin-singlet fractional quantum Hall edges in graphene
articles.excerpt_original: The edge modes of spin-singlet fractional quantum Hall (FQH) phases are manifestations of multicomponent topological order and SU(2) spin symmetry. An archetype is the spin-unpolarized state at $ν$=2/3, whose edge is expected to host spatially coexisting yet counter-propagating charge and neutral spin modes. Despite efforts, its edge properties, including spin coherence and spin-charge separation, have remained elusive owing to the difficulty of resolving spins in FQH edge transport. Here, we develop a spin-sensitive probe of graphene FQH edges by using a p-n junction to interface a target FQH state with a probe integer quantum Hall (QH) state of opposite polarity. An Aharonov-Bohm (AB) interferometer forms along the interface, when the target and probe edge channels carry the same spin. We identify the spin-unpolarized and polarized edges of the $ν$=2/3 states at lower and higher magnetic fields, respectively, through spin-dependent interference. A novel multiparticle AB interference between two electrons of opposite spin emerges from spin-charge separation and recombination on the unpolarized edge, featuring a spin swap. Our results establish edge transport as a probe of spin-singlet topological orders, with implications for parafermion platforms in graphene-superconductor hybrids.
articles.summary_en: Researchers developed a spin-sensitive Aharonov–Bohm interferometer using graphene p–n junctions to distinguish spin-unpolarized and spin-polarized ν=2/3 fractional quantum Hall edge states. The observation of multiparticle interference and spin-charge separation could inform graphene–superconductor parafermion platforms.

articles.title_original: A critical review of MXene and MXene/polymer composites: Structure-Property relationships, applications, and data-driven perspectives
articles.title_en: Review Maps MXene–Polymer Composite Design and Applications
articles.excerpt_original: MXenes have emerged as a highly versatile class of two-dimensional materials with exceptional electrical conductivity, flexibility, and hydrophilicity. Integrating MXene with polymers has unlocked extensive opportunities for various applications. This review discusses the preparation methods of MXenes and their polymer composites and critically analyzes the structure-property relationships that govern their performance in sensors, supercapacitors, and electromagnetic interference shielding. The potential of these composites in biomedical and other cutting-edge applications is also explained. Additionally, the role of emerging tools, such as machine learning and density functional theory calculations, is highlighted as promising approaches for accelerating the development and application directions of MXenes and their composites. Furthermore, this review discusses the associated challenges and offers future perspectives for advancing the potential of these materials. Overall, this review aims to critically summarize existing efforts and provide a platform for researchers seeking to develop high-performance MXene/polymer composites.
articles.summary_en: A critical review examines how MXene structure and polymer integration influence performance in sensors, supercapacitors, electromagnetic-interference shielding and biomedical applications. It highlights machine learning and density-functional-theory modelling as tools to accelerate materials optimisation, while noting unresolved preparation and scale-up challenges.

articles.title_original: BN/MXene nanosheets-based cementitious composite materials with enhanced properties
articles.title_en: h-BN/MXene Cement Composites Improve Strength and Durability
articles.excerpt_original: : Cementitious composites generally suffer from low tensile strength, poor toughness, and insufficient durability, which significantly compromise their structural integrity and stability and shorten service life. To address these drawbacks, two-dimensional nanomaterials are innovatively introduced as admixtures for fabricating cementitious composites in this work. Within the composite matrix, hexagonal boron nitride (h-BN) and MXene generate synergistic effects via pore filling, hydration product refinement, microcrack bridging and hydration acceleration, greatly densifying and homogenizing the matrix to comprehensively improve the composite performance. The obtained hybrid specimen containing 0.5 wt% h-BN and 0.5 wt% MXene displays excellent integrated properties over the pristine and single-doped specimens, with tensile strength, compressive strength and impermeability increased by 12.7%, 40.4% and 80.7%, respectively, alongside remarkable improvements in thermal stability and fire resistance. Among single-doped groups, the specimen modified with 1.0 wt% h-BN achieves a 65 % improvement in flexural strength, whereas the sample filled with 0.5 wt% MXene delivers a 16 % enhancement in compressive strength. Although existing theoretical simulations predict considerable strengthening potential for functionally graded composites reinforced with two-dimensional nanofillers, these quantitative predictions cannot be directly transferred to reactive cementitious systems. This study provides quantitative experimental data on mechanical and durability enhancements originating from synergistic h-BN/MXene modification. It validates the feasibility of employing 2D nanofillers to reinforce cementitious matrices and offers a new pathway for developing next-generation high-performance
articles.summary_en: Researchers developed cementitious composites incorporating hexagonal boron nitride and MXene nanosheets, with a hybrid formulation increasing tensile strength, compressive strength and impermeability by 12.7%, 40.4% and 80.7%, respectively. The material also showed improved thermal stability and fire resistance, indicating potential for higher-performance construction materials.

articles.title_original: Thermal Stability of Ti3C2Cl2, Ti3C2Br2, and Ti3C2I2 MXenes Probed by In Situ Synchrotron XRD
articles.title_en: Synchrotron XRD Study to Probe Thermal Stability of Halogen-Terminated MXenes
articles.excerpt_original: MXenes are single- or multilayer two-dimensional (2D) transition metal carbides and nitrides that have attracted significant attention due to their tunable surface chemistry and outstanding physical properties. Among them, halogen-terminated MXenes have recently emerged as a particularly promising type of materials because of their high chemical stability and uniform surface coverage achieved via synthesis in Lewis acid molten salts. The aim of this proposal is to investigate the thermal stability of halogen-terminated Ti3C2Tx MXenes (Ti3C2Cl2, Ti3C2Br2, and Ti3C2I2) under controlled argon and air atmospheres using in situ high-temperature synchrotron X-ray diffraction.
articles.summary_en: Researchers propose using in situ high-temperature synchrotron X-ray diffraction to examine Ti3C2Cl2, Ti3C2Br2, and Ti3C2I2 MXenes under argon and air. The work targets thermal stability and degradation behavior of halogen-terminated two-dimensional materials synthesized in Lewis acid molten salts.

articles.title_original: Calcium/magnesium ferrites-incorporated MXene for As(III) removal from aqueous solution
articles.title_en: Ferrite-Functionalized MXene Enhances Arsenic Removal
articles.excerpt_original: Arsenic ranks first among the carcinogenic 1 group of heavy metals. Various techniques have been employed to remove the contaminants from aqueous media, with adsorption being the most suitable. For this purpose, the emerging material, MXene and its functionalized forms with calcium ferrites and magnesium ferrites have been used. The hydrothermal method was adopted for the synthetic purposes. For structure, morphology, magnetic behavior, surface area and functional group determination, X-ray diffraction, field emission scanning electron microscopy, transmission electron microscopy, vibrating sample magnetometer, Barrett–Joyner–Halenda, and Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy were employed. For adsorption studies, batch tests were conducted with the effects of pH, contact time, temperature, and concentration. The pseudo-second-order kinetics (R2 ≈ 0.98), along with Langmuir and Freundlich isotherms (R2 ≈ 0.98) were found well fitted to the experimental data. Among the synthesized adsorbents, MXene, MXene functionalized with calcium ferrite, and MXene functionalized with magnesium ferrite demonstrated monolayer adsorption capacities of 1829, 4399, and 4631 µg/g, respectively. Ultimately, the reusability of materials was investigated through desorption analyses.
articles.summary_en: Researchers developed calcium- and magnesium-ferrite-functionalized MXene adsorbents for removing As(III) from water. The magnesium ferrite composite achieved the highest reported monolayer adsorption capacity at 4,631 µg/g, outperforming calcium ferrite-functionalized MXene and unmodified MXene.

articles.title_original: Mn-doped 2D hexagonal boron nitride: Boosting supercapacitor performance via point defects
articles.title_en: Mn-Doped Boron Nitride Improves Supercapacitor Performance
articles.excerpt_original: Hexagonal boron nitride (h-BN) is chemically robust but intrinsically insulating, which limits its direct use as an electrochemically active electrode material. Structural and defect evolution were investigated using XRD, Raman spectroscopy, photoluminescence (PL), and electron paramagnetic resonance (EPR). PL reveals a systematic enhancement of blue emission with increasing processing severity, consistent with the creation of dopant- and defect-related radiative recombination pathways and concomitant band-structure perturbation. EPR directly confirms Mn incorporation through the M n 2 + hyperfine sextet and shows temperature-dependent linewidth broadening, indicating stronger Mn–Mn interactions and partial clustering at higher annealing temperatures, while a carbon-related signal near 𝑔 ≈ 2 . 0 0 5 is suppressed upon annealing. For this best-performing composition, the maximum specific capacitance reaches 566.73 F/g at a scan rate of 10 mV/s, and the Ragone plot yields an energy density of 78.7 Wh/kg at a power density of 15.7 kW/kg. articles.summary_en: Researchers developed manganese-doped hexagonal boron nitride with defect engineering that produced a pronounced pseudocapacitive response. The best composition reached 566.73 F/g specific capacitance and 78.7 Wh/kg energy density at 15.7 kW/kg power density.

articles.title_original: Tuning Boron-Vacancy Qubit Coherence through Layer Number in hBN
articles.title_en: Layer number tunes hBN boron-vacancy qubit coherence
articles.excerpt_original:
The negatively charged boron vacancy ($\VB$) in hexagonal boron nitride (\hBN{}) was the first optically addressable spin qubit identified inside a van der Waals crystal, allowing atomically defined placement relative to a target. Its coherence in bulk \hBN{} is limited by the boron nuclei of the layers flanking the defect plane, which a thin flake removes. Here, we use a generalized cluster-correlation expansion with an extended central-spin block to calculate the Hahn-echo coherence time of $\VB$ in h$^{11}$B$^{15}$N as a function of layer number. Our results show that $T_2$ rises from $199
s$ in the bulk limit to $653
s$ in a monolayer, a factor of $3.3$ that is already saturated at three layers and that a sublattice decomposition attributes entirely to boron. The enhancement is confined to low field, is insensitive to stacking registry and twist angle, and requires alignment to within about two degrees, an onset we reproduce with no free parameters. Under dynamical decoupling, a $1/e$ threshold returns $206
s$ for every thickness, but this is a zero of the first-shell modulation rather than a decay: measured without a threshold, the layer contrast survives and reaches a factor of $170$. Layer number thus emerges as a design parameter for $\VB$-based sensing.
articles.summary_en: A theoretical study finds that reducing hexagonal boron nitride to a monolayer increases boron-vacancy qubit Hahn-echo coherence from 199 ns in bulk material to 653 ns. The results identify layer number as a design parameter for quantum sensing, with the enhancement dependent on low-field alignment.

articles.title_original: Fabrication of Boron Nitride@Polydopamine/Polyvinyl Alcohol/Polyvinylidene Fluoride Composite Film With Good Thermal Stability and Thermal Conductivity via Electrospinning and Hot Pressing Treatment
articles.title_en: BN–PDA Polymer Composite Film Demonstrates Enhanced Thermal Conductivity
articles.excerpt_original: The field of thermal conductivity is one of the important applications of polymers. However, polymer material generally possesses low thermal conductivity due to its internal characteristic, which cannot meet the heat dissipation requirement of device. Therefore, the preparation of polymer material with high thermal conductivity has broad application prospect and important significance. To achieve this goal, a new‐type composite film was fabricated via electrospinning and hot pressing treatment. Utilizing the self‐polymerization of dopamine under alkaline condition, polydopamine (PDA) was deposited on the surface of boron nitride (BN). The obtained BN@PDA acted as filler for polyvinyl alcohol (PVA). In addition, polyvinylidene fluoride (PVDF) was introduced into PVA through coaxial spinning. The results indicated that the thermal conductive filler was uniformly distributed and well adhered on the fiber. Moreover, thanks to the intermolecular force between PVA and PVDF, the acquired composite film had good thermal stability with the decomposition temperature over 300 °C. On the other hand, the got composite film exhibited good thermal conductivity at low filling ratio. It could quickly transfer the heat generated during the operation of the LED light, which could reduce the operating temperature of the equipment in actual use, demonstrating its good heat dissipation capability.
articles.summary_en: Researchers fabricated a boron nitride–polydopamine/PVA/PVDF composite film using electrospinning and hot pressing. The film showed thermal stability above 300 °C and efficiently dissipated heat from operating LEDs at low filler loading.

articles.title_original: Light metal functionalized two-dimensional carbon nitride (C6N7) monolayers for efficient hydrogen storage
articles.title_en: Metal-Functionalized C6N7 Monolayers Show Promise for Hydrogen Storage
articles.excerpt_original: This study investigates light metal-decorated carbon nitride (C 6 N 7 ) monolayers for hydrogen (H 2 ) storage using density functional theory (DFT). Compared with previously explored theoretical carbon nitride materials, this work focuses on experimentally synthesized C 6 N 7 , providing a realistic platform with verified chemical and thermal stability. Since pristine C 6 N 7 exhibits weak H 2 adsorption, Na, K, and Ca are introduced as dopants to enhance storage performance. The stability of the metal-decorated systems is confirmed by ab initio molecular dynamics simulation, while binding energies are evaluated against the cohesive energies of the corresponding bulk metals. Charge transfer and projected density of states analyses reveal strong metal-C 6 N 7 interactions and enhanced electronic polarization. The optimized systems achieve gravimetric storage capacities of 12.87, 11.67, and 11.61 wt% and volumetric capacities of 63.14, 59.76, and 69.14 g/L for Na-, K-, and Ca-functionalized C 6 N 7 , respectively. Moderate H 2 adsorption energies (−0.17 to −0.18 eV/H 2 ) indicate favourable reversibility for practical hydrogen storage.
articles.summary_en: DFT simulations indicate that sodium-, potassium-, and calcium-functionalized C6N7 monolayers could deliver hydrogen capacities of 11.61–12.87 wt% with reversible adsorption energies. The study uses experimentally synthesized, chemically and thermally stable C6N7 as a realistic theoretical platform.

articles.title_original: 1D Plasticity in Semiconductor Crystals
articles.title_en: 1D Plasticity Enables Shape-Conformable Thermoelectric Generators
articles.excerpt_original: The exceptional plasticity recently found in inorganic semiconductors can be classified into two types: the three-dimensional (3D) orientation-insensitive deformability in polycrystals, and the two-dimensional (2D) anisotropic case in layered crystals. It is thus highly anticipated that one-dimensional (1D) plasticity should also exist but it has not been found yet. Here this work reports the excellent 1D plasticity in tin selenide (SnSe) semiconductor crystals. In in-plane directions, the bending strain is as large as ∼22.7% for the zig-zag-aligned specimen (plasticity) while as small as ∼1.4% for the armchair-aligned one (brittleness). Such 1D plasticity is ascribed to the coherent and stronger bond topology along b-axis that allows for multiple deformation mechanisms including layer segments, interlayer slip, bridging, lattice distortion, and dislocations. This bonding topology enables that the 1D plasticity is also observed in isostructural SnS and GeSe crystals. High-performance shape-conformable thermoelectric generators are then successfully developed using materials with 1D plasticity. This work enriches the diagram for plasticity and thus provides a new direction for the design and discovery of ductile semiconductors.
articles.summary_en: Researchers report pronounced direction-dependent plasticity in tin selenide crystals, with related behavior also observed in SnS and GeSe. The materials enabled high-performance, shape-conformable thermoelectric generators, suggesting a route to more ductile semiconductor devices.

articles.title_original: Near‐Infrared and Short‐Wave Infrared Two‐Dimensional PbSe/PbS Heterostructures With Lead Halide Perovskite Passivated Surface for Light‐Emitting Diode
articles.title_en: Perovskite-Passivated PbSe/PbS Heterostructures Enable NIR/SWIR LEDs
articles.excerpt_original: Near‐infrared (NIR) light sources based on colloidal two‐dimensional (2D) semiconductor heterostructures hold significant promise for biomedical imaging and optical communications, yet their practical deployment is constrained by surface trap‐mediated nonradiative decay and poor solid‐state stability. Herein, we report a solution‐processable interfacial passivation strategy for PbSe/PbS core/shell and core/wings nanoplatelets using a mixed‐halide CsPb(Br/I) 3 perovskite matrix. Comprehensive structural and spectroscopic analyses demonstrate that the perovskite overlayer effectively suppresses surface defects, yielding a 2.3–2.7× enhancement in relative photoluminescence intensity and extending emission lifetimes to 3.8 ns while preserving the intrinsic NIR/short‐wave infrared (SWIR) emission profiles. When integrated into solution‐processed devices, the passivated films enable down‐conversion light‐emitting diodes (LEDs) with radiance of up to 0.026 W/sr/m 2 under 450 nm excitation, as well as charge‐injection LEDs exhibiting a low turn‐on voltage of ~4.1 V and electroluminescence at 1310 and 1610 nm. This work establishes a robust surface‐engineering framework that bridges colloidal 2D lead chalcogenide heterostructures with practical solid‐state optoelectronics, paving the way for novel NIR/SWIR emitters.
articles.summary_en: Researchers developed a solution-processable mixed-halide perovskite passivation layer for 2D PbSe/PbS nanoplatelets, suppressing surface defects and improving photoluminescence intensity by 2.3–2.7×. The treated films enabled down-conversion and charge-injection LEDs emitting at 1310 and 1610 nm, supporting potential optical communications and imaging applications.

articles.title_original: Recent Advances in True Random Number Generators Based on Emerging Material-Based Semiconductor Devices: Toward Wearable and Flexible Electronics
articles.title_en: Review Examines Emerging-Material True Random Number Generators
articles.excerpt_original: As technologies such as artificial intelligence, autonomous driving, the Internet of Things, wearable electronics, and edge computing continue to spread in the era of the Fourth Industrial Revolution, the importance of hardware security for the safe storage, transmission, and processing of large volumes of data has grown substantially. One of the key components of such security systems is the true random number generator (TRNG), which produces unpredictable random numbers for cryptographic use. In recent years, research on TRNGs has increasingly moved beyond conventional CMOS-based approaches toward semiconductor devices built from emerging materials. These material-based TRNGs offer several advantages, including high integration density, low power consumption, compact form factors, and strong suitability for next-generation edge and IoT environments, because they can directly exploit the intrinsic stochasticity of the device itself as an entropy source. In this review, recent studies on TRNGs based on emerging material-based semiconductor devices are examined from the perspectives of entropy sources, device structures, randomness validation, and wearable/flexible extensions. By bringing together the key physical mechanisms, device platforms, evaluation criteria, and prospects for wearable and flexible electronics in edge and IoT environments, this review aims to provide a useful framework for future research on hardware security devices.
articles.summary_en: This academic review surveys true random number generators built from emerging-material semiconductor devices, focusing on entropy sources, device architectures, randomness validation, and wearable or flexible extensions. It highlights potential benefits for hardware security in edge, IoT, and next-generation electronics, but reports no specific commercial product or company.

articles.title_original: Space‐Confined Kinetic Growth of Thick 2D Perovskite Single Crystals for High‐Performance X‐Ray Detection
articles.title_en: Space-confined growth enables thick 2D perovskite crystals for improved X-ray detection
articles.excerpt_original: ABSTRACT Two‐dimensional (2D) perovskites have emerged as promising scintillators for ultrafast X‐ray imaging due to their unique quantum confinement effects. However, their intrinsic thermodynamic growth habits, driven by highly anisotropic chemical bond strengths, typically restrict crystals to thin, plate‐like morphologies, which limits their X‐ray stopping power and overall light yield. Here, we report a space‐confined kinetic manipulation strategy to circumvent the conventional thermodynamic thickness limitations, enabling the growth of macroscopically thick phenethylammonium lead bromide single crystals (PEA 2 PbBr 4 SCs). By reallocating chemical potential gradients and maintaining a stable metastable window, we successfully accelerated longitudinal growth along the ( 00l ) facets, achieving crystals with thicknesses exceeding 3.2 mm and a low lateral‐to‐longitudinal aspect ratio (<3). The resulting SCs exhibit exceptional structural quality, and the enhanced X‐ray attenuation in these thick SCs leads to a superior light yield of 37 500 photons MeV −1 , doubling that of the thin counterparts (0.6 mm, 15 224 photons MeV −1 ). This work provides a robust pathway for synthesizing thick 2D perovskite SCs for high‐performance radiation detection and imaging without compromising their inherent exciton confinement advantages.
articles.summary_en: Researchers developed a space-confined kinetic strategy to grow phenethylammonium lead bromide 2D perovskite single crystals thicker than 3.2 mm. The crystals achieved a reported light yield of 37,500 photons MeV−1, approximately double that of 0.6 mm counterparts, supporting higher-performance X-ray imaging.

articles.title_original: Ultralow Friction in Graphene Multilayers with Amorphous Carbon Interlayers
articles.title_en: Amorphous Carbon Interlayers Reduce Friction in Graphene Multilayers
articles.excerpt_original: Amorphous carbon layers (ACLs) have been experimentally realized as a two-dimensional carbon material, but their influence on sliding in graphene multilayers is still unclear. In this study, molecular dynamics simulations were carried out for pristine graphene (PG) multilayers and graphene/amorphous-carbon (AG) multilayers under normal pressures of 0.1, 1, and 10 GPa. Both models show ultralow friction. The coefficient of friction (COF) decreases with increasing pressure because the friction force increases much more slowly than the normal force. AG has lower COF than PG at all pressures, with reductions of about 60%, 54%, and 26%, respectively. Layer displacement and interlayer sliding analyses show that shear in PG is transferred through several graphene/graphene interfaces, whereas relative sliding in AG is mainly located near the ACLs. Under high pressure, the ACLs become flatter, which may help stabilize local sliding. These results suggest that amorphous carbon interlayers may modify shear transfer and facilitate ultralow-friction sliding in graphene-based multilayers under the present simulation conditions.
articles.summary_en: Molecular dynamics simulations found ultralow friction in both pristine graphene and graphene/amorphous-carbon multilayers under pressures of 0.1–10 GPa. Amorphous-carbon interlayers reduced the simulated coefficient of friction by approximately 26–60% by localizing interlayer sliding and stabilizing shear under pressure.

articles.title_original: Fluorine-19 NMR Spectroscopy as a Strong Analytical Tool for the Development of PFAS Waste Management Strategies in Semiconductor Manufacturing
articles.title_en: 19F NMR Advances PFAS Waste Management in Semiconductor Manufacturing
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract Per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) are environmentally persistent, mobile, and bioaccumulative compounds with demonstrated toxicity, often linked to endocrine disruption, liver damage, cancer, and developmental risks. Semiconductor manufacturing facilities or fabs rely on the use of PFAS in some of their equipment components and materials. Photolithography patterning performance is often enhanced by fluorinated photoacid generators in photoresists, low-index fluoropolymers in anti-reflective coatings, and fluorosurfactants. Since these materials are frequently released in fab waste, they inform the abatement and characterization needs evaluated in this review. In this article, we discuss 1D/2D NMR methods, quantitative NMR (qNMR), proper selection of solvents and internal standards, strategies for managing dilute samples in fabs, PFAS abatement techniques and 19F NMR implications, and integrated analytical methods for PFAS characterization. 19F NMR is a strong tool that can provide non-target and class-specific analysis, measure total organic fluorine, and, more importantly, allow for rapid screening of waste streams before and after treatment, thereby providing fab-specific guidance on PFAS treatment techniques and ultimately assisting with the long-term aspiration of phasing out PFAS-containing materials. Such capabilities make 19F NMR a valuable metrology tool for PFAS detection, quantification, and sustainable waste management in fabs. Furthermore, novel 19F NMR methods with enhanced sensitivity can further decrease detection limits and allow for the characterization of highly dilute samples, often pertaining to fab waste.
articles.summary_en: A review assesses fluorine-19 NMR as a rapid, non-targeted method for detecting and quantifying PFAS in semiconductor-fabrication waste streams. The approach could guide treatment evaluation and support efforts to phase out PFAS-containing materials in fabs.

articles.title_original: pH-controlled assembly of graphene oxide membranes with nitrogen-doped graphene quantum dots for enhanced nanofiltration performance
articles.title_en: pH-Controlled Graphene Oxide Membranes Enhance Nanofiltration
articles.summary_en: The study investigates pH-controlled assembly of graphene oxide membranes incorporating nitrogen-doped graphene quantum dots. It reports enhanced nanofiltration performance, relevant to advanced water-treatment membrane design.

articles.title_original: Tunneling characteristics of twisted double bilayer graphene heterostructures
articles.title_en: Twisted bilayer graphene shows tunable resonant tunneling and negative differential resistance
articles.excerpt_original: Electron tunneling between sheets of bilayer Bernal graphene twisted at different small angles was studied experimentally and theoretically. The current-voltage characteristics exhibit resonant peaks, steps, and regions of negative differential resistance, the origin of which is explained by the intersections of energy- and momentum-shifted electron dispersions of adjacent layers. A theoretical analysis of tunneling transport demonstrated that the key to understanding this phenomenon lies in the competition between two contributions: between like (conductivity-conductivity or valence-valence) and unlike (conductivity-valence) bands of parallel bilayer graphene sheets. A systematic evolution of the tunneling current patterns with increase of the twist angle is investigated. Polarization of electron wave function across graphene sublayers caused by displacement field within bilayer graphene is shown to strongly affect the tunneling probability, thus enhancing negative differential resistance due to Van Hove singularities at the band edges.
articles.summary_en: Experimental and theoretical work examines electron tunneling between slightly twisted Bernal graphene bilayers. The study identifies resonant peaks, steps, and negative differential resistance, with twist angle, band alignment, Van Hove singularities, and displacement-field-induced wave-function polarization controlling transport.

articles.title_original: Unpassivated edges as gateways to collision-driven topological transformations in finite graphene nanoflakes
articles.title_en: Simulations Show How Unpassivated Graphene Edges Drive Collision-Induced Transformations
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract Finite graphene nanoflakes occupy a unique position in the carbon allotrope landscape. Near equilibrium, these systems exhibit pronounced structural robustness, indicating that large-scale allotropic transformations require strongly non-equilibrium energy deposition. In this work, we investigate how unpassivated graphene edges act as chemically active gateways for collision-driven topological transformations in finite graphene systems. Using reactive molecular dynamics simulations, we model energetic collisions involving a C $$_{60}$$ 60 fullerene projectile and a finite C $$_{296}$$ 296 graphene nanoflake across a broad parameter space of collision energies, incidence angles, and edge orientations. The structural response is analysed through statistical transformation maps that quantify the probability of nanoflake bending, edge stitching, and the formation of nanotube-like structures. We identify a regime of collision energies and oblique incidence angles under which localised energy deposition at unpassivated edges promotes bond rearrangement, cooperative bending, and covalent stitching between opposing edges. Furthermore, we find that armchair-directed impacts align opposing zigzag edges and promote efficient edge-to-edge stitching over a broader parameter range. In contrast, zigzag-directed impacts are associated with a higher probability for atom ejection and bring opposing armchair edges into contact, which is less favourable for seam propagation, resulting in a narrower parameter window for nanotube-like structure formation. These results establish a non-equilibrium framework linking local edge chemistry and collision-induced energy deposition to topological evolution in finite graphene systems. The results demonstrate collision-driven self-organisation
articles.summary_en: Reactive molecular-dynamics simulations indicate that unpassivated edges enable bond rearrangement, bending, and covalent stitching in finite graphene nanoflakes struck by C60 molecules. Collision energy, incidence angle, and edge orientation determine whether flakes form nanotube-like structures or undergo atom ejection.

articles.title_original: Synthesis, Characterization, and Application of 2D MXene Nanosheets for Surfactant-Assisted Enhanced Oil Recovery
articles.title_en: MXene–Surfactant Nanofluids Improve Enhanced Oil Recovery
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract Nanomaterial-based enhanced oil recovery (EOR) has emerged as a promising alternative to conventional chemical flooding techniques for improving oil recovery under harsh reservoir conditions. To address thermal instability, salinity sensitivity, and adsorption losses associated with traditional surfactants, this study developed a hybrid nanofluid system based on MXene and containing surfactants sodium dodecyl sulfate and cetyltrimethylammonium bromide (SDS and CTAB). The layered shape and surface functions of titanium carbide MXene (Ti3C2Tx) were validated using XRD, FTIR, field-emission scanning electron microscopy (FESEM), high-resolution transmission electron microscopy (HRTEM), AFM, and XPS investigations. The compound was synthesized by selectively etching and delaminating the MAX phase. Investigations into the stability of colloidal particles revealed remarkable dispersion behavior at a concentration of 600 ppm, with a zeta potential of –35.6 mV and almost no aggregation. The incorporation of CTAB and SDS significantly enhanced the dispersion stability of MXene, making the nanofluid more suitable for EOR applications. For CTAB-MXene systems, the interfacial tension between crude oil and water was very low at 0.1–0.15 mN/m, whereas for SDS-MXene systems it was 2.1 mN/m. Oil mobilization and displacement efficiency were improved by the stable oil–water emulsions produced by the hybrid nanofluids, which also exhibited strong emulsification capacity. However, the emulsion stability decreased marginally with increasing salinity. Measurements of the contact angle showed a significant change in wettability, from an oil–wet to a strongly water–wet state (<10°). articles.summary_en: Researchers developed titanium carbide MXene nanofluids containing SDS or CTAB surfactants to improve dispersion stability, reduce oil–water interfacial tension, and alter reservoir wettability. Core-flooding results indicated enhanced oil mobilization and displacement efficiency, although emulsion stability declined slightly with increasing salinity.

articles.title_original: Powdered MXene-integrated magnetic hydrogel for the high-capacity adsorption and rapid separation of microplastics from water
articles.title_en: MXene Hydrogel Enables Rapid, High-Capacity Microplastic Removal
articles.excerpt_original: Microplastics pose a persistent threat to aquatic ecosystems, driving interest in magnetic hydrogel adsorbents. However, conventional Fe₃O₄-based systems suffer from iron leaching during reuse, creating secondary pollution. MXene addresses this limitation and additionally enhances interfacial interactions with target pollutants. Although MXene-hydrogel composites have been reported for heavy metals, dyes, and pharmaceuticals, to our knowledge this is the first report of a magnetic MXene-alginate composite for microplastic capture. We therefore compared a baseline Alginate/Polyvinylpyrrolidone/Fe₃O₄ composite (M1) with its MXene-reinforced counterpart (M2), each in bead and powdered forms, for removing polypropylene (PP), polystyrene (PS), and polyethylene terephthalate (PET) microplastics (5–75 μm). Beads showed poor removal (<40%) regardless of composition, whereas powdered forms performed markedly better (96%) due to greater exposed surface area and closer size matching with the target MPs. Within the powdered format, M2 raised removal from 30.83 ± 3.62% to 48.6 ± 7.50% (PP), 65.83 ± 5.18% to 76 ± 4% (PS), and 70.8 ± 4.7% to 96.2 ± 1.45% (PET). This same reinforcement also resolved M1's iron leaching (6.86 ± 0.46 mg L − 1 , above the WHO aesthetic guideline of 2 mg L − 1 ), reducing it below threshold at pH 6. Under these conditions, powdered M2 achieved 486 ± 14.1, 760.33 ± 17, and 962.34 ± 8.02 mg g − 1 for PP, PS, and PET, equilibrating within 15 min, with performance retained across tap, lake, and seawater and 75 ± 3.5% capacity after six regeneration cycles, positioning powdered MXene-reinforced magnetic alginate hydrogel (M2) as a practical platform for microplastic remediation.
articles.summary_en: Researchers developed a powdered MXene-reinforced magnetic alginate hydrogel that removed up to 96.2% of tested microplastics and reduced iron leaching below the stated threshold. The material retained 75% of its capacity after six regeneration cycles and worked across tap, lake, and seawater, highlighting potential for water remediation.

articles.title_original: Ultrathin nano-layered boron nitride stabilizing perovskite quantum dot-based light-emitting diodes
articles.title_en: Ultrathin Boron Nitride Extends Perovskite QLED Lifetime
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract Perovskite quantum dot-based light-emitting diodes (QLEDs) have been regarded as promising emitters for lighting and displays. However, the operational stability still greatly hinders their practical applications. Here, we introduce ultrathin nano-layered boron nitride (BN) as buried interfacial layer to enhance device stability. As an effective blocking layer, BN not only interacts with perovskite to passivate interface defects and eliminate ion migration channel, but also directly suppresses ion migration. Meanwhile, BN makes exciton recombination behavior and electrical transport properties of perovskite QDs less sensitive to the heat. Resultantly, BN-optimized QLEDs achieved an average EQE of 30.05% and extrapolated operational lifetime T 50 of 25,263 h at an initial luminance ( L 0 ) of 100 cd m −2 , which is 1.7-fold and about 100-fold improvement compared to control devices, respectively. In this work, integrating 2D materials into perovskites through interface engineering provides a pragmatic tactic to enhance the performance of halide perovskite-based LEDs.
articles.summary_en: Researchers used ultrathin layered boron nitride as a buried interface layer to passivate defects and suppress ion migration in perovskite quantum-dot LEDs. articles.title_original: Natural Light Emission via Quantized Anderson Localized States in 2D Amorphous Semiconductor Heterojunctions
articles.title_en: 2D Amorphous Semiconductor Heterojunctions Proposed for Full-Spectrum White Light
articles.excerpt_original: ABSTRACT Nowadays, the full‐spectrum artificial lighting technology that approaches the solar spectrum has become an important issue in the field of lighting. Yet, to date, the development of full‐spectrum white‐light‐emitting diodes (WLEDs) remains hindered by the fixed band gaps of conventional semiconductors and the synthetic challenges of certain specific‐color phosphors, resulting in poor spectral tenability and far deviation from the solar spectrum. Herein, based on first‐principles calculations, we propose a new conceptual scheme to potentially achieve full‐spectrum white light emission via two‐dimensional (2D) amorphous heterojunction (a‐SiC/a‐MoS 2 ), which intrinsically emits broadband white light closely matching the D65 standard source. We further reveal that the underlying mechanism of full‐spectrum emission stems from two aspects: firstly, the quantum confinement effects in 2D amorphous heterojunctions lead to the formation of a series of discrete and strongly localized Anderson tail states in their bandgaps; secondly, the disordered structure breaks the orbital symmetry, which fully enables transitions of these states that maybe forbidden in crystalline counterparts. Thus, the combined effect of the two not only allows for sufficient transition energy levels, but also modulates the spectral distribution. Our work opens a new approach for full‐spectrum artificial lighting, with promising implications for the advancement of high‐quality lighting.
articles.summary_en: Researchers use first-principles calculations to propose an amorphous SiC/MoS₂ heterojunction that could emit broadband white light closely matching the D65 standard. articles.title_original: A viable and accurate route to GW simulations of metals and doped semiconductors
articles.title_en: Efficient GW Method Improves Simulations of 2D Metals and Doped Semiconductors
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract In this work, we present an efficient and fully ab initio approach for the calculation of the screened Coulomb potential, specifically designed for two-dimensional (2D) and three-dimensional (3D) metals and suitable to evaluate G W corrections. While quasiparticle renormalization effects are typically negligible in bulk metals, 2D metals may exhibit semiconductor-like features, such as sizeable renormalization of quasiparticle energies induced by Coulomb interaction, which follow from the suppression of screening due to the reduced dimensionality. Although this effect can in principle be described by the G W method, apart from a few pioneering exceptions, such calculations have been hampered by sampling requirements exceeding feasibility. We demonstrate that the combination of interpolation and extrapolation schemes together with the accounting of dynamical effects is pivotal to the correct handling of the intraband polarizability in the long-wavelength limit. As an application, we report the gap renormalization of selected doped 2D semiconductors in excellent agreement with ARPES measurements.
articles.summary_en: Researchers present an efficient first-principles approach for calculating screened Coulomb interactions and quasiparticle corrections in two- and three-dimensional metals. The method addresses long-wavelength screening and reproduces gap-renormalization results for doped 2D semiconductors in agreement with ARPES measurements.

articles.title_original: Strain Engineering of Two-Dimensional Penta-Octa B4C2N3: Electronic Structure and Optical Response
articles.title_en: Strain-Tunable 2D B4C2N3 Shows Promise for Optoelectronics
articles.excerpt_original: Two-dimensional (2D) boron–carbon–nitrogen (BCN) systems have recently attracted significant interest owing to their structural stability, electronic diversity, and tunable optical behavior. In this work, the structural, electronic, and optical properties of the 2D penta–octa B4C2N3 monolayer are systematically investigated using first-principles calculations. The optimized structure exhibits moderate buckling, multiple distinct bond environments, and energetically favorable cohesive and formation energies. The monolayer is identified as a non-magnetic indirect semiconductor with a band gap of 0.279 eV, where the density of states is dominated by N–p and C–p orbitals. Thermal stability is confirmed by ab initio molecular dynamics simulations at 600 K, and a relatively high work function of 5.272 eV suggests strong surface stability and favorable compatibility with electronic interfaces. Biaxial strain is shown to be highly effective in tuning the electronic structure. Compressive strain (-4% to -2%) induces a semiconductor-to-metal transition, while moderate tensile strain (+1% to +3%) results in an indirect to direct band gap conversion. The band gap can be continuously tuned from 0.11 eV to 0.583 eV under tensile loading. Optical absorption calculations reveal strong light–matter interaction with absorption coefficients reaching 104–105 cm-1. These results demonstrate that 2D penta–octa B4C2N3 is a structurally robust, electronically adaptive, and optically responsive monolayer with strong potential for next-generation strain-engineered optoelectronic and photonic devices.
articles.summary_en: First-principles calculations identify penta–octa B4C2N3 as a stable, non-magnetic semiconductor with strong optical absorption. Applied strain can switch it between semiconductor and metallic states and tune its band gap, indicating potential for strain-engineered optoelectronic and photonic devices.

articles.title_original: Halogenated Ti2C MXene: A promising multifunctional 2D material for optoelectronic and thermoelectric applications — Predictions from DFT
articles.title_en: Halogenated Ti2C MXenes Predicted for Optoelectronic and Thermoelectric Applications
articles.excerpt_original: Two-dimensional (2D) MXenes have attracted significant attention owing to their remarkable electronic, optical, and thermoelectric (TE) characteristics, making them promising candidates for advanced multifunctional devices. In this work, the structural stability and physical properties of pristine and halogen-functionalized (-F, -Cl, -Br, and -I) Ti 2 C MXenes were systematically investigated using first-principles based density functional theory (DFT) calculations. The electronic band structure (EBS) and projected density of states (PDOS) analyses reveal that pristine Ti 2 C exhibits metallic behaviour, which is retained even after surface functionalization with halogen atoms. The cohesive energy (E C ) calculations confirm the thermodynamic stability of all studied systems, as evidenced by their negative E C . Among them, I-functionalized Ti 2 C shows the highest stability with an E C of approximately −6.05 eV. Halogenation of Ti 2 C significantly modifies its optical response, lowering the static refractive index from about 6–7 in pristine Ti 2 C to roughly 2–4 and shifting the main optical features into the 1.5–3.5 eV range. The extinction coefficient also changes, with the strong low-energy peak of pristine Ti 2 C (∼20) becoming broadened and termination-dependent, indicating altered interband transitions and optical loss. Surface functionalization of Ti 2 C effectively modulates their TE properties, inducing a carrier type transition from n-type (pristine and F-terminated) to p-type (Cl and Br-terminated). Notably, fluorine functionalization yields the highest room-temperature power factor of 1.93 × 10 12 Wm −1 K −2 s −1 due to an optimized Seebeck coefficient (-1.29 ×10 −4 V/K) and a significantly suppressed thermal conductivity of 0.19 × 10 15 Wm −1 K −1 s −1 .
articles.summary_en: DFT calculations indicate that halogen functionalization can tune Ti2C MXene stability, optical response, carrier type, and thermoelectric performance. The findings identify fluorinated Ti2C as having the highest reported room-temperature power factor among the studied systems, while chlorine and bromine terminations induce p-type behavior.

articles.title_original: A Unified Description of Dirac-Cone Anisotropies in Two Dimensions
articles.title_en: Unified Framework Describes Dirac-Cone Anisotropies in Graphene
articles.excerpt_original: Anisotropies in two-dimensional materials are responsible for a variety of effects that significantly modify their physical properties. In this paper, we present a covariant modification of the Dirac equation that incorporates anisotropies into the effective low-energy description around the Dirac point. The model is constructed by analogy with a Lorentz-violating extension of the Standard Model of elementary particles and yields a (2+1)-dimensional framework describing physical effects such as shifted, tilted, and distorted Dirac cones through its free parameters. The proposed model thus provides a general and unified framework in which distinct anisotropy-induced modifications of the Dirac spectrum and their combinations can be systematically characterized. We further apply the model to strained graphene and show that its effective parameters can be quantitatively extracted from first-principles electronic band structures while retaining a direct geometrical interpretation. These results establish a connection between the microscopic electronic structure and a material-independent effective description of anisotropic two-dimensional Dirac systems.
articles.summary_en: Researchers propose a covariant model for characterizing shifted, tilted, and distorted Dirac cones in two-dimensional materials. Applied to strained graphene, the framework links first-principles band structures with geometrically interpretable effective parameters.

articles.title_original: First-Principles Electronic Structure Calculation of Crystals in Laboratory Magnetic Fields
articles.title_en: New First-Principles Method Simulates Graphene in Laboratory Magnetic Fields
articles.excerpt_original: External magnetic fields can qualitatively reshape the electronic structure of crystals, underpinning quantum Hall physics, Landau-level spectra and field-induced topological phases. Their first-principles treatment at laboratory-scale fields is, however, hindered by magnetic-flux quantization, which requires magnetic unit cells with areas inversely proportional to the applied field. Such cells contain a large number of chemical unit cells, rendering real-space and plane-wave calculations prohibitively expensive. Here we, for the first time, construct a magnetic Bloch basis built from linear combinations of gauge-including Gaussian-type atomic orbitals, which incorporate the magnetic-field phase factors required by magnetic translation symmetry. The framework requires far fewer basis functions than real-space or plane-wave representations of the same magnetic supercell and retains the sparsity of an atom-centred basis, together substantially reducing computational cost. We validate the framework by reproducing Landau-level spectrum of graphene from first principles. This approach provides a practical route to simulations of crystalline materials under experimentally accessible magnetic fields.
articles.summary_en: Researchers developed a magnetic Bloch-basis framework that reduces the computational cost of modeling crystals under experimentally accessible magnetic fields. The method reproduces graphene’s Landau-level spectrum from first principles, supporting studies of quantum Hall and field-induced topological phenomena.

The optimized MX@Alg film exhibited a remarkable tensile strength of 107.68 ± 1.39 MPa and an impressive Young’s modulus reaching 2232 ± 58.03 MPa, representing increases of approximately 14% and 32%, respectively, compared with pristine alginate film, while maintaining excellent film flexibility. In addition, water vapor permeability (WVP) was reduced by 35.7%, indicating improved barrier performance. articles.title_original: Boron nitride nanotube fibers with over 1 GPa strength and 1000 °C stability for exceptional neutron shielding textiles
articles.title_en: BNNT–CNT Fibers Enable High-Strength Neutron-Shielding Textiles
articles.excerpt_original: Integrating boron nitride nanotubes (BNNTs) into robust macroscopic architectures for deep space radiation shielding remains a fundamental challenge. Here, we report continuous self-assembled all-nanotube (SAAN) fibers with an 80 wt% BNNT loading, combining tensile strength exceeding 1 GPa with extreme thermal stability from −196 to 1200 °C. These fibers originate from the thermodynamic co-assembly of BNNTs and carbon nanotubes (CNTs) into a lyotropic liquid crystalline mesophase. This shear-responsive dope enables cooperative reorientation and dense nanotube packing during wet-spinning. When assembled into macroscopic textiles, SAAN exhibits an exceptional thermal neutron attenuation coefficient of 2.85 mm−1. Furthermore, computational simulations indicate these lightweight textiles can effectively mitigate highly penetrating secondary thermal neutrons generated by Galactic Cosmic Ray (GCR) spallation. Demonstrating their seamless integration into commercial 2D flat and 3D tubular textile manufacturing processes, this nanomanufacturing approach provides a scalable and reliable strategy for space radiation shielding in both intravehicular (IVA) and extravehicular (EVA) activities. Researchers developed continuous, flexible boron nitride nanotube fibers achieving over 1 GPa strength and 1,000 °C stability. Interwoven into lightweight textiles, they provide thermal neutron shielding for potential manned deep space missions.

articles.title_original: Layer-selective and magnetic-field-enhanced transport of topological kink states in rhombohedral multilayer graphene
articles.title_en: Magnetic fields enhance topological transport in multilayer graphene
articles.excerpt_original: Topological valley kink states (VKSs), which are quantum valley Hall states emerging at the interfaces between adjacent domains with opposite valley Chern numbers, have attracted considerable interest in graphene-based systems. In this work, we investigate the quantum transport of VKSs in ABC-stacked rhombohedral multilayer graphene in the presence of Anderson disorder and a perpendicular magnetic field. Two prominent transport characteristics are revealed. First, in the absence of a magnetic field, the kink states exhibit strong layer polarization, with their wave functions predominantly localized and equally distributed on the outermost top and bottom layers. As a result, their transport properties are highly sensitive to the layer-selective disorder distribution. Second, under a perpendicular magnetic field, the layer-symmetric spatial distribution of VKSs is broken, leading to a significant reduction in the wave-function overlap between counter-propagating VKSs from opposite valleys. Consequently, intervalley scattering is suppressed, and the transmission of VKSs through disordered regions is substantially enhanced. Our results provide new insights into multichannel topological valley transport in rhombohedral multilayer graphene and demonstrates disorder-engineering and magnetic fields as effective approaches for manipulating the propagation of VKSs.
articles.summary_en: ArXiv research finds that rhombohedral multilayer graphene’s valley kink states are strongly layer-polarized and sensitive to layer-selective disorder. articles.title_original: MOSFET Device Structures and Physical Models: A Historical Review
articles.title_en: Historical Review of MOSFET Structures and Physical Models
articles.excerpt_original: This article traces the progress of the metal–oxide–semiconductor field-effect transistor (MOSFET) device structure and physical models over the past century. While the concept of a field-effect transistor (FET) was conceived early on, the realization of a physical MOSFET had to wait until the interface state problem was solved in 1960. Subsequently, the evolution of MOSFET device structure has been driven by the needs to mitigate parasitic capacitance and resistance, and to maximize packing density. A revolutionary change of the MOSFET structure took place in 2011 when FinFET was introduced by forming a double-gate MOSFET over a thin silicon film perpendicular to the wafer plane. On the modeling front, gradual channel approximation (GCA) was employed from the very beginning to simplify the 2D partial differential equation of potential to a 1D ordinary differential equation, valid for long channel MOSFETs. Further simplification includes the charge sheet model and regional approximations that render explicit, but piecewise I–V relations of a MOSFET. Separately, short-channel MOSFET models have been developed by solving the 2D boundary value problem in the subthreshold region. It developed scale length equations capable of predicting the minimum channel length of a MOSFET for a given oxide thickness and substrate doping concentration. For symmetric double-gate MOSFETs with negligible doping, the 1D Poisson's equation of potential is analytically solvable to yield all-region I–V relations in terms of implicit equations.
articles.summary_en: This academic review traces MOSFET development from early field-effect concepts through FinFET structures and evolving physical models. It examines approaches for managing parasitic effects, scaling channel dimensions, and deriving current–voltage relationships across operating regimes.

articles.title_original: Graphene Oxide‐Metal Nanoparticle Interactions and Their Application in Melamine Sensing
